captions.text: Your class can choose one library display theme.
How can we make a recommendation that listens to the class?
Imagine a display table waiting for a new library theme.
A bright idea is useful, but the class should have a voice in the choice.
We can use an investigation to move from a question to evidence, and from evidence to a recommendation that explains its limits.
Today we are learning to conduct an investigation and communicate a careful conclusion.
Our goal is to complete an investigation and communicate a careful conclusion.
We will connect the skills from the earlier lessons.
The final report should explain the question, who answered, how responses were checked, what the display shows and which decision the evidence can support.
I can pose a useful question and collect relevant checked data.
I can choose a display and interpret its mode and shape.
I can report evidence, a limitation and a sensible next question.
Recall the different jobs we have practised.
A fair question collects relevant information.
A frequency table counts checked responses.
A column graph compares category counts.
The mode identifies a most common choice.
Now we will bring those pieces together, with context and a next step.
Use a cycle: question → plan → collect → check → display → interpret → communicate.
Name the group, keep the collection fair and record one anonymous response per pupil.
Choose a column graph for named choices, ordered columns for ratings or counts, and a line graph for change over time.
A sample tells us about those asked; do not automatically speak for the whole school.
Begin by naming the decision and the group.
Our question asks which library theme this class would choose.
The allowed choices are Animals, Space, Sport and Other.
Club names and theme names are nominal categories: they have no natural order.
A column graph will compare frequencies; a line joining themes would wrongly suggest a time sequence.
We want to know which theme our class prefers: animals, space or sport.
Is “You love space, don’t you?” a fair survey?
Before collecting anything, compare the two possible survey questions.
Does either one suggest that a particular answer is expected?
Think about how you would feel if your favourite were different.
Choose wording that lets pupils answer honestly, and keep your reason ready.
Ask “Which of these themes would you choose?” using the same options for everyone, with another option too.
Ask all class members once, allow a private response and record no names in the report.
A collection plan should say when the class will respond, how each pupil will be counted once, and what happens if someone is away.
